title: Daily Health Briefing
intro: Good morning! Today's digest spans your five tracked topics — anti-aging, HIIT for women, pelvic floor training, HER2+/TP53 breast cancer options, and sleep. It leans on recent, reputable work from JAMA Network Open, PubMed, NIH/ClinicalTrials.gov, Frontiers, AASM, and the integrative-oncology guidelines; citations are linked as chips under each section. Informational only — talk to a clinician before acting on anything here.

sections.topic: Anti-Aging — mTOR Trials, NAD+ & Light Devices
sections.body:
The through-line this week: the serious longevity science is moving into **well-designed human dose-finding trials**, while the consumer wins are in **at-home light devices** with real (if modest) data.

- **Rapamycin/rapalogs — the human dosing work is finally happening.** UT Health San Antonio, funded by the **NIH/National Institute on Aging**, launched the **RESTOR** trial (NCT06658093) in March 2026 — a randomized, placebo-controlled study in ~84 adults aged 65–90 to pin down a safe dose and schedule of **rapamycin (sirolimus)** and **everolimus**. Notably, investigators expect the **optimal dose to differ by sex**, so both men and women are enrolled. A separate UT Southwestern/NIA study (NCT06727305) is tracking a **senescence (SASP) biomarker** score at 3 months.
- **Everolimus healthspan readout due.** The **EVERLAST** RCT (NCT05835999) testing daily vs. weekly low-dose everolimus on metabolic, cardiac, cognitive, and physical aging in insulin-resistant adults 55–80 is wrapping up (primary completion Sept 2026) — one of the first gold-standard looks at whether a rapalog safely improves aging hallmarks in humans.
- **NAD+ boosters, measured expectations.** A Brigham/NIA phase-2 RCT of **NMN** (1 g twice daily) in diabetic kidney disease (NCT05759468) is also tracking aging biomarkers (IL-6, TNF-α) — useful signal on whether NAD+ repletion does more than raise lab values.
- **At-home red-light masks.** A multicenter, **randomized, double-blind, sham-controlled trial** of a 630 nm LED + 850 nm near-infrared mask significantly improved **crow's-feet wrinkles** vs. a sham device, and a 12-week British Journal of Dermatology in-use study showed measurable gains in skin **elasticity and resilience**. Effects are gradual and need ongoing use — a reasonable, low-risk adjunct to **retinoids** and sunscreen.

Practical framing: favor interventions with human RCTs, expect **modest** effects, and don't self-prescribe rapalogs off-label while the dosing trials are still running.

sections.body:
A new **2026 systematic review & meta-analysis** (*Frontiers in Physiology*) sharpens the picture for women — HIIT is a strong **cardio** tool, but you should **add resistance training** for strength and function.

- **Big cardio win, in older women too.** Pooling **19 RCTs (646 middle-aged and older women)**, HIIT significantly improved **VO₂max** vs. controls (SMD = 1.20; 95% CI 0.86–1.54) with *high* certainty, and the benefit held across age, body-mass status, and program length.
- **But not a strength fix.** In the same analysis, HIIT did **not** significantly improve **muscle strength**, flexibility, or sit-to-stand, and walking ability improved only borderline. Translation: HIIT builds the engine; **lift weights** to build strength and preserve function.
- **Women respond as well as men.** A Sports Medicine meta-analysis (965 adults) found **equivalent VO₂max gains** in women and men from HIIT (g ≈ 0.57 each), and well-trained women actually out-gained men on peak power — reassurance that intensity pays off regardless of sex.
- **Dose matters.** Across reviews, **longer HIIT intervals** and **more total sessions** drive bigger VO₂max gains than very short protocols — consistency beats any single "magic" interval scheme.

Bottom line: use HIIT 2–3×/week for cardiometabolic health, **pair it with 2×/week strength work**, progress gradually, and protect recovery.

sections.body:
**Pelvic floor muscle training (PFMT)** stays the evidence-based, **first-line** approach for stress urinary incontinence (SUI). New 2026 trials focus on *prevention*, *supervision*, and *adherence*.

- **Train during pregnancy to prevent leakage later.** A **multicenter JAMA Network Open RCT** (764 first-time mothers across 9 hospitals) tested **PEFLOW** — PFMT blended with global postural exercise — started in early pregnancy. SUI at 6 weeks postpartum fell to **8.7% vs 13.9%** in controls, and far more women reached a strong pelvic-floor contraction (MOS ≥4: **17.8% vs 7.9%**). Prevention, not just treatment, works.
- **Supervision beats going solo.** A 2026 RCT (60 women) found **supervised PFMT** cut pad-test leakage from ~23 g to ~3 g and got **66.7%** to Oxford grade 4–5 strength, vs. only **13.3%** with unsupervised home training — though unsupervised remains a reasonable option when adherence is good and resources are limited.
- **Adherence is the hidden lever.** A 2026 *BMC Women's Health* trial of a **"5E" self-management model** raised 12-week PFMT adherence to **74% vs 32%** and reduced incontinence episodes more than routine care — reinforcing that *doing the exercises correctly and consistently* is what drives results.

Key point: get your technique confirmed (clinician or biofeedback), favor **supervised or structured** programs, and build a routine you'll actually keep.

sections.topic: Alternative & Integrative Options — HER2+ / TP53 Breast Cancer
sections.body:
For HER2-positive disease — where **TP53/p53 mutations are the norm, not the exception** — "alternative" is best read as **evidence-based integrative care *alongside* standard HER2-targeted therapy**.

- **TP53 status doesn't blunt the best drug.** A biomarker analysis of the phase-3 **DESTINY-Breast03** trial found **TP53 altered in ~73%** of HER2+ metastatic tumors — yet **trastuzumab deruxtecan (T-DXd)** kept its large advantage over T-DM1 **regardless of TP53, PIK3CA, HRD, or BRCA status**. Reassuring for anyone with a p53-mutant tumor: the standard-of-care still works.
- **A rational combo target on the horizon.** Preclinical work in *J Exp Clin Cancer Res* showed that pairing T-DXd with a **DNA-repair (ATR) inhibitor** overcame resistance in HER2+ models — a mechanistic rationale (not yet a treatment) worth watching as trials open.
- **Integrative therapies with real evidence.** The **SIO guideline endorsed by ASCO** supports **exercise, yoga, meditation, music therapy, and acupuncture/acupressure** for anxiety, mood, fatigue, quality of life, and chemo nausea. A 2025 living guideline adds **strong** backing for exercise (pain, QoL) and mind-body work.
- **Where "natural" claims fall short.** In a 686-patient RCT, oral **curcumin did not reduce radiation dermatitis**; **high-dose vitamin C, vitamin E, and selenium** are *not* recommended; **oral mistletoe** can be dangerous and isn't FDA-approved; and **short-term/fasting-mimicking diets** show only mixed, limited evidence and shouldn't be done unsupervised during treatment.

Important framing: integrative options are **add-ons to discuss with your oncology team** — never substitutes for HER2-targeted therapy — and several supplements can **interact** with treatment.

sections.body:
For restless or disjointed sleep, 2026 guidance keeps **behavioral therapy ahead of pills** — and is refreshingly honest about what supplements can and can't do.

- **CBT-I first, combos second.** The **AASM's 2026 clinical practice guideline** on combination therapy concluded CBT-I **plus** medication beats **medication alone**, but is **not** better than **CBT-I alone** — because CBT-I delivers durable gains without drug risks. Reserve medications as a short-term adjunct.
- **Magnesium — small but real.** The largest trial to date (randomized, double-blind, 155 adults with poor sleep) found **250 mg elemental magnesium as bisglycinate** daily modestly lowered **Insomnia Severity Index** scores vs. placebo by week 4 (effect small, Cohen's d ≈ 0.2), with the **biggest benefit in people low in dietary magnesium**. The co-delivered **glycine** may itself aid sleep onset.
- **Melatonin: right tool, narrow job.** AASM recommends **against** melatonin for chronic insomnia; it's best for **circadian problems** — jet lag and shift work — and effective doses are **low (0.3–0.5 mg)**, far below typical 5–10 mg products. **Ashwagandha** has modest, stress/cortisol-driven data; **L-theanine** may help "busy brain."

Best-practice habits for disjointed sleep:

1. Hold a **fixed wake time**, even weekends.
2. Keep the bed **for sleep only**; room cool, dark, quiet.
3. **Screens off ~1 hour** before bed; get **morning sunlight** within an hour of waking.
4. If disruption persists beyond a few weeks, see a provider to rule out **sleep apnea** and consider **CBT-I** (in-person or digital).
